markers.title: One way in, and it is a verb
markers.finding: The platform assumed a team member would scan a poster and fill in the form. In practice they told the manager, who logged it or did not, so the manager is the heaviest user of the system.
markers.decision: The manager's primary action is the same action the team member gets on a phone: Report something. It sits above the navigation, not inside a module, so logging on someone's behalf is one click from anywhere.
markers.rejected: A New incident button inside the Incidents module, which makes the reporter choose the record type before they have described anything.

markers.title: Sorted by what needs a person, not by record type
markers.finding: Reports sat waiting because nothing told the manager which ones needed them today; the platform's lists were organised by the record's type rather than by whether anyone was waiting.
markers.decision: The first tile is Needs your review, counted across incidents and hazards together, with the reason written underneath in words a manager reads once.
markers.rejected: A tile per module (incidents, hazards, actions) which reports the shape of the database rather than the shape of the shift.

markers.title: Fixes are counted, and so is where they came from
markers.finding: Minor reports were closed without a word, and over time people came to believe that reporting helps with a claim but changes nothing. The restaurant where a fault was fixed the same day had a story people kept telling.
markers.decision: Fixed this period is a headline number, split to show how many came from the team's own reports. It is the number the manager repeats at the huddle.
markers.rejected: Counting reports received, which rewards volume. The safety team's view was that an incentive on hazard reports gets you reports, not fewer hazards.

markers.title: Two series, because the ratio is the signal
markers.finding: Reporting volume varied widely between restaurants, and low volume could mean a safe restaurant or a silent one. The platform's data could not tell the difference.
markers.decision: Hazards and incidents are plotted side by side every week. A restaurant finding hazards before they hurt anyone looks different from one that reports only after an injury, and the reading is written under the chart in a sentence.
markers.rejected: A single total-reports line, which is the number that could not distinguish a safe restaurant from a silent one.

markers.title: The status is the next human act
markers.finding: The form asked for incident type and severity first, with options like first aid or lost time that nobody can pick while their hand is under the cold tap, and classification errors were sent back from above.
markers.decision: A report's status names what a person does next: welfare check due, action assigned, fixed and awaiting sign-off. Classification is an outcome the manager records later, so it never blocks the report.
markers.rejected: Status as a workflow code (open, triaged, pending classification), which describes the database's state rather than anyone's obligation.

markers.title: The loop, closed on the manager's screen
markers.finding: Reporters rarely heard what happened after they reported, and minor reports were closed silently.
markers.decision: A standing panel names each fix, who reported it and how long it took, with one action that prints the notice for the break room. Telling people is a default, not a task someone remembers.
markers.rejected: A monthly email to the reporter, which depends on a mailbox most team members do not read on shift.

markers.title: Hazards located, because the blueprint located them
markers.finding: Every observation in the research was tied to a stage of the incident journey and to the role it concerned, which is what let the findings point at exact places in the service rather than at themes.
markers.decision: Hazards are counted by area of the restaurant, so the pattern points at the fryer line or the back door rather than at a category name.
markers.rejected: A hazard-type breakdown, which sorts by the taxonomy the reporter was never able to apply.

markers.title: The routine is part of the product
markers.finding: Where a manager talked about safety, thanked people for reports and showed the system on the first shift, reporting was strong regardless of where the restaurant was. Induction varied from a full demonstration to nothing.
markers.decision: Today's shift carries the routine the research found to be the strongest lever: a safety moment drawn from this week's reports, the new starter's first-shift walkthrough, the first-aid cabinet check.
markers.rejected: Leaving the routine to a separate training system, which is where it lived when nobody could tell whether a new starter had been shown the system.
